role.text: In view because this Story happens here.
In 1590 the Jesuits printed a book here that describes the trade.
A Dutchman in Goa heard that Portuguese and Chinese people lived here together and traded with Canton.
Historians date the Portuguese settlement to 1557.
A Venetian at Malacca was told the customs here belonged to the king of China.
People bought in Japan were brought here. The Church's record of 1598 says some fled into China.
The marker shows present-day Macao; it is not a surveyed position for the town of 1590.
The coast drawn is today's. How it lay in 1590 is not researched.

A Japanese historian writes that the port was opened in 1570.

entities.historicalName: The yearly ship from Macao to Japan

connection.directionNote: Macao to Nagasaki and back, across the East China Sea. Silk and gold one way, silver the other. Directional; not symmetric.
connection.directionFigureText: Portuguese merchants of Macao  →  enabled  →  Nagasaki, for silver

spatial.targetText: Nagasaki · settlement precision · named as the usual port by Linschoten, who was never there
spatial.routeStatement: Each year a Portuguese ship sailed from Macao to Japan with Chinese silk and gold, and came back with silver. The Ming court barred its own merchants from trading with Japan, and Japan's new mines had silver to spend. The reports we have were written far from the ship: by an Englishman at Malacca in 1588, by a Dutchman at Goa, and in a Jesuit book printed at Macao in 1590. No Source we have read names the ship, its captain or its cargo for 1590. The same ship carried people who had been bought in Japan.
spatial.accountsSentence: The same ship carried people who had been bought in Japan.

connection.scholarlyStanding: Kobata (1965), Atwell (1982) and von Glahn (1996) all describe this trade as Chinese silk for Japanese silver, with the Portuguese as carriers between two countries that could not trade openly. They do not agree on how much silver it moved, and Kobata says Japan's output cannot now be calculated. Flynn (1991) argues that the mines' profits helped one lord unify Japan; he offers it as a hypothesis.

mechanismText.text: Japan's mines had been producing silver in large amounts since the 1530s.
Japan wanted Chinese silk above all.
The Ming court kept its ban on trade with Japan when it reopened the sea in 1567.
The Portuguese at Macao could buy at Canton and sail to Japan, so they carried the silk.
One ship a year was licensed for the voyage, by Linschoten's account, and it used Nagasaki. A historian's count has two sailings in 1590.
It came back with nothing but silver, by two reports made at Malacca and Goa.
Gold went out on the same ship, because gold bought more silver in Japan than in China.
How much silver came back is not known. The modern estimates go back to a figure an English merchant was told at Malacca.
This is how the Portuguese of Macao came to supply Nagasaki for silver. The Claims it rests on are listed beneath it. None of the European reports was made at Macao.

participants.text: Portuguese merchants of Macao, who bought at Canton and sailed to Japan
The captain of the Japan ship, who held the voyage by the king's licence and governed Macao while there
Chinese sellers at Canton, who are named by no Source we have read
Chinese officials, who took the customs at Canton and kept the Portuguese out of the city at night
The Ming court, which kept the ban on trade with Japan
The Jesuits at Macao, who printed the book that describes the trade
Crews, among them a Dutch gunner, Dirck Gerritsz
People bought in Japan and carried to Macao, boys and girls among them

connection.evidenceIndependenceNote: Three European reports, none made at Macao, and they are not fully independent. Fitch and Linschoten were in Goa at the same time: Linschoten's editor says Fitch was brought there a prisoner soon after Linschoten arrived. Linschoten's account of China is taken largely from an earlier printed book, his editor says. The Macao book and its English translation are one witness, not two. The modern historians all start from these same reports. No Chinese or Japanese Source from the time is among them. On the people carried, the Sources are the Church's own papers.

reverseDisclosure.body: Silver from Nagasaki to Macao and on to Canton is the other half of this trade, and it is in this Connection's Claims. What that silver did inside China, and what the silk did inside Japan, are different Connections with their own Sources. They are not researched here.

connection.reverseRelationshipNote: A separate Connection, not an inversion of this one.

handover.privacyNote: This report goes by email to the site's editor through Web3Forms, a form service run from India. It is not public. Web3Forms says it keeps submissions for up to three years unless they are deleted sooner. To catch spam, it may send your IP address, and your email if you leave one, to the spam filters CleanTalk and Akismet. The editor also sees your IP address, in the email that carries your report. You will not be asked to tick a box. The editor keeps your report until it has been dealt with and for 90 days after, then deletes it, including the copy held at Web3Forms. To remove your credit or your data, choose "Remove my credit or my data" in the first question of the form, and say in "Anything else" which preferred name or email. Please do not include anyone else's personal details. A person reads the reports we receive. We aim to reply within a week if you left an email. Checking a Source can take weeks, because we read it ourselves, through a library. What you report cannot change the page by itself; only a Source we have read can. jurisdictionLine.text: Reports from the years before 1590 describe Macao as a town where Portuguese and Chinese people lived. A Venetian at Malacca was told that its customs belonged to the king of China and were paid at Canton. A Dutchman at Goa wrote that the captain of the Japan ship ruled the town while he was there. Which jurisdiction it lay in has not been researched, so none is shown and no boundary is drawn.

body: Select the Event on the map, or in the list beneath it, to open its Story.

This Moment is Macao about 1590: the ship that sailed each year to Japan, and the one Connection this pilot explains for it, Portuguese merchants of Macao and the trade at Nagasaki, silk for silver. Nagasaki is drawn at the wider view as the port a Dutchman at Goa names. One part of the Story is about people who were bought in Japan and carried on the same ship.

segments.text: We don't know how many people were carried. The Church's record says a great number every year and gives no figure.
We don't know that people were carried on the ship of 1590, or of any one year. The papers describe what was done year after year, three years before and eight years after.
We don't know their names, where in Japan most of them came from, or what happened to most of them after Macao.
We have almost none of their own words. What we have was written down by churchmen, about their own conduct.
People from China and Korea were bought and carried on the same routes. That is not researched here.
We don't know which year the Macao book means by 'this present year'. It was licensed in September 1589.
We don't know how much silver the ship brought back. The modern estimates all go back to a figure told to an English merchant at Malacca and to two Jesuits' reports.
We don't know who sold the silk at Canton. No Chinese merchant speaks in anything we have read.
We have no words from the miners, from the lords who held the mines, or from the merchants of Kyushu.
We know almost nothing of the Chinese people who lived in Macao. One Dutchman in Goa mentions them in a clause.
